target.title: Speech Synthesis from ECoG using Densely Connected 3D Convolutional Neural Networks
target.version: Author manuscript (available in PMC 2020-06-01); final edited form published 2019-03-04; first public as bioRxiv 10.1101/478644 v1 (2018-11-27, wiki doi-10.1101-478644)

entries.text: The proposed pathway maps ECoG from speech-production areas to logMel spectrograms, then vocodes the predicted representation to an audible waveform.
entries.condition: Overt speech production; DenseNet is fit separately for each participant and WaveNet is a separately trained vocoder.

entries.text: The authors claim dense connectivity is well suited to the extremely small participant-specific training sets.
entries.condition: Authors' motivation for the participant-specific DenseNet regression model; not an ablation against alternative architectures in this study.

entries.text: The cohort comprised six native-English-speaking participants undergoing awake craniotomy for brain-tumor resection; participants had normal speech, language, and hearing.
entries.condition: Clinical cohort undergoing awake craniotomies for brain tumor resection; all were motor-intact with normal speech/language function and hearing.

entries.text: ECoG was acquired with a 64-channel 8 × 8 medium-density grid with 4 mm electrode spacing.
entries.condition: Integra grid; 8 × 8 layout; 4 mm spacing; implanted for the awake craniotomy recordings.

entries.text: The grid covered ventral motor cortex (M1v), premotor cortex (PMv), and inferior frontal gyrus pars opercularis (IFG); placement was guided by landmarks and direct cortical stimulation.
entries.condition: Speech articulatory sites; grid locations varied by participant.

entries.text: ECoG was sampled at 2 kHz.
entries.condition: Neuroport data acquisition system; 64-channel ECoG during overt word production.

entries.text: Reference acoustic speech was recorded with a unidirectional Sennheiser lapel microphone at 48 kHz.
entries.condition: Simultaneously recorded overt speech used as acoustic reference and logMel target source.

entries.text: Participants read 244–372 words each, producing recordings 8.5–12.7 minutes long.
entries.unit: words per participant; minutes per recording
entries.condition: Single-word reading task during each participant's awake-craniotomy session; individual participant values are not paired in the text.

entries.text: The elicitation task was reading aloud single words displayed on screen; words were predominantly monosyllabic consonant-vowel-consonant forms and mostly drawn from the Modified Rhyme Test.
entries.condition: Overt, cued single-word speech; not continuous or imagined speech.

entries.text: ECoG preprocessing included linear detrending and a 60-Hz line-noise notch (118–122 Hz, elliptic IIR, order 13).
entries.unit: Hz line frequency; Hz notch band; filter order
entries.condition: Applied to ECoG before broadband-gamma feature extraction.

entries.text: Broadband-gamma features used 70–170 Hz power, estimated as mean squared signal in 50-ms windows with 10-ms overlap, then log transformed.
entries.condition: Filter orders 13 and 14 are reported for the broadband-gamma band; log transform was used to make the feature distribution more Gaussian.
entries.quote: Broadband-gamma power was extracted in 50 ms windows with an overlap of 10 ms.

entries.text: Broadband-gamma activity was normalized separately for each electrode to zero mean and unit variance.
entries.condition: Per electrode; the paper does not say whether normalization statistics were estimated on training data only or on all available recording data.

entries.text: Nine temporal contexts were stacked, spanning up to 200 ms into both past and future; each window was represented as an 8 × 8 × 9 tensor.
entries.unit: temporal contexts; ms each direction; feature dimensions
entries.condition: 64 electrodes arranged to preserve the participant-specific grid topography; temporal offsets are centered around each decoding window.
entries.quote:
This results in a feature space of size 64
electrodes
× 9
temporal offsets
.

entries.text: Acoustic targets were downsampled to 16 kHz; phase was discarded and magnitude spectra were represented by 40 logarithmic mel bins using 50-ms windows with 10-ms overlap.
entries.unit: kHz; bins; ms window; ms overlap
entries.condition: Mel mapping used triangular filter banks; the resulting logMel spectrogram was the DenseNet regression target.

entries.text: DenseNet maps spatio-temporal broadband-gamma activity to logMel coefficients per participant; the separate WaveNet maps predicted spectral features to audio without a participant-specific ECoG mapping.
entries.condition: Two-stage cascade: participant-specific ECoG-to-spectrogram model, followed by vocoder trained on a larger corpus.
entries.quote: This was done for each participant individually, as electrode grid placements and underlying brain topologies are vastly different between participants.

entries.text: DenseNet used three dense blocks with two sublayers each, 3 × 3 × 3 convolutions, 20 initial feature maps, growth rate 10, and 80 total feature maps; the linear output had 40 neurons.
entries.value: 3 blocks; 2 sublayers/block; kernel 3 × 3 × 3; 20 initial maps; growth 10; 80 maps; 40 outputs
entries.condition: 3D convolutions and pooling over the 8 × 8 × 9 ECoG feature tensor; regression to 40 mel coefficients.

entries.text: The DenseNet regression model had around 83,000 trainable parameters.
entries.condition: Per-participant 3D DenseNet for ECoG-to-40-bin-logMel regression.
entries.quote: Overall, our resulting network comprises around 83,000 trainable parameters.

entries.text: DenseNet training minimized mean-squared error with Adam for a fixed 80 epochs.
entries.condition: Per-participant regression; the paper does not report a DenseNet learning rate, batch size, or weight decay.

entries.text: WaveNet was trained on LJ-Speech, a separate single-speaker corpus of readings from seven nonfiction books.
entries.condition: Separate corpus for the acoustic vocoder, not the six-participant ECoG dataset.

entries.text: LJ-Speech utterances were 1–10 seconds long, totaling around 24 hours.
entries.condition: Single-speaker LJ-Speech training corpus used for the WaveNet vocoder.
entries.quote: The length of an utterance varies between one and ten seconds and sums up to a total amount of around 24h of speech data.

entries.text: The WaveNet vocoder autoregressively predicts each next audio sample from prior samples in its receptive field and the local conditioning spectrogram.
entries.condition: Autoregressive waveform generation conditioned on logMel features; current implementation is reported as too slow for real-time synthesis.

entries.text: The vocoder used 30 residual blocks, three dilation cycles, and a 10-component mixture of logistic distributions; conditioning features were upsampled through four transpose convolutions.
entries.unit: residual blocks; dilation cycles; mixture components; transpose convolutions
entries.condition: WaveNet acoustic waveform generator conditioned on logMel features.

entries.text: Table 1 lists 512 residual channels, 256 skip connections, an approximately 0.5-second receptive field, and 30 residual blocks.
entries.condition: WaveNet vocoder hyperparameters; residual and skip channel counts refer to the vocoder network.

entries.text: WaveNet training used Adam with initial learning rate 0.001 for 600,000 update steps.
entries.condition: Separate LJ-Speech vocoder training; article does not report a WaveNet training/test split or random seed.

entries.text: For each participant, recorded data were divided into disjoint train/test sets using 5-fold cross-validation; 20% of training data were reserved as validation data.
entries.condition: Within-participant evaluation; the paper says validation was reserved to analyze optimization but does not state a checkpoint or hyperparameter selection rule.
entries.quote: For each participant, we partitioned the recorded data into disjoint sets for training and testing in a 5-fold cross validation.

entries.text: Pearson product-moment correlation was computed separately for each frequency bin between reconstructed and original spectrograms.
entries.condition: The reported participant means and standard deviations average over logarithmic mel coefficients; this is spectrogram correlation, not waveform correlation.
entries.quote: The correlations are computed for each frequency bin individually between the reconstructed spectrogram and its original counterpart.

entries.text: The chance baseline randomly split each recording at a time point, swapped the partitions to break ECoG–spectrogram alignment, and retrained using 5-fold cross-validation.
entries.condition: Each participant's chance level was estimated 60 times using unique temporal splits; the neural signal structure was preserved while alignment was shifted.
entries.quote: For each participant, we repeated the estimation of a random chance level 60 times

entries.text: Participant 1's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.19 ± 0.12.
entries.condition: Participant 1; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: Participant 2's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.29 ± 0.06.
entries.condition: Participant 2; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: Participant 3's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.56 ± 0.18.
entries.condition: Participant 3; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: Participant 4's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.34 ± 0.12.
entries.condition: Participant 4; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: Participant 5's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.69 ± 0.10, the best participant result.
entries.condition: Participant 5; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.

entries.text: Participant 6's mean Pearson correlation across logMel coefficients was 0.41 ± 0.07.
entries.condition: Participant 6; per-frequency-bin original/reconstructed logMel correlation, averaged over coefficients; within-participant 5-fold cross-validation.
entries.quote:

entries.text: The authors report correlations significantly above their randomized chance baseline for all six participants (p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Six participant-specific 5-fold evaluations compared with the authors' randomized temporal-split chance baseline; statistical test procedure is not specified.

entries.text: Participant 5 clearly outperformed the other participants; the authors hypothesize that electrode placement captured articulator-related information better.
entries.condition: Post hoc explanation, explicitly presented as a hypothesis rather than a tested mechanism.

entries.text: STOI intelligibility was evaluated against the original experiment audio; the paper plots participant scores but gives no numerical STOI values in the text or table.
entries.condition: Waveform intelligibility metric; Fig. 5c is a bar plot, with no exact scores printed in the article text/table.

entries.text: The STOI chance comparison used the randomized spectrogram exceeding 95% of the randomizations to generate the comparison waveform.
entries.condition: Chance waveform generated with the WaveNet vocoder; original experiment audio served as STOI reference.
entries.quote: For the chance level, we took the randomized spectrogram that was better than 95% of the randomization to estimate a waveform using the Wavenet vocoder.

entries.text: The authors characterize the reconstructed audio as high quality and say reconstructed words are often intelligible; this is a qualitative claim, not a reported word-recognition score.
entries.condition: Overt single-word production; selected examples and supplementary audio are shown/listed.
entries.quote: The resulting audio is of high quality and reconstructed words are often intelligible.

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first high-quality speech reconstruction from speech-production neural recordings using deep neural networks.
entries.condition: Novelty claim is scoped to high-quality audio reconstructed from neural recordings during speech production using DNNs; paper cites an earlier direct-synthesis pilot study.
entries.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that high-quality speech has been reconstructed from neural recordings during speech production using deep neural networks.

entries.text: The authors claim that conditioning WaveNet on a much larger pre-existing corpus provides the most natural acoustic output.
entries.condition: Separate-corpus WaveNet vocoder; the paper does not report a quantitative naturalness or speaker-similarity score.
entries.quote: The vocoder was conditioned on logMel features that harnessed a much larger, pre-existing data corpus to provide the most natural acoustic output.

entries.text: Prior cited work had reconstructed perceived speech from ECoG and spectral dynamics of speech from ECoG.
entries.condition: The text cites references 28 and 29 for auditory-cortex speech reconstruction and ECoG spectral-dynamics reconstruction, respectively.

entries.text: For context, the authors state traditional speaker-dependent speech systems use dozens of training hours, while high-performing speaker-independent systems accumulate thousands.
entries.condition: General background comparison in speech processing; not a measured baseline in this study.

entries.text: As motivation, the authors cite >50 ms as too slow for a recognition-then-synthesis speech pipeline; this is a prior-work statement, not a measurement of their proposed system.
entries.condition: Two-step speech recognition followed by text-to-speech for real-time scenarios; references 21–22.

entries.text: The current method is offline and not suitable for real-time use because of computational complexity.
entries.condition: Current DenseNet-plus-WaveNet implementation; no closed-loop operation was evaluated.

entries.text: DenseNet optimization is time-consuming and exceeds the recording time of a typical experimental session.
entries.condition: Training-time limitation for the participant-specific regression model; no quantitative runtime is reported.

entries.text: The current WaveNet implementation cannot generate acoustic output in real time.
entries.condition: Waveform synthesis stage; no real-time latency or throughput value is reported.

entries.text: The study used overtly produced speech from motor-intact participants; the authors say more research is needed for paralyzed patients, with attempted and imagined speech only prospective extensions.
entries.condition: No attempted- or imagined-speech decoding was evaluated in this study.

entries.text: Evaluation is within participant: each participant's data are split and a model is fit individually; the paper does not report held-out-participant generalization.
entries.condition: Speaker/participant identity is shared across each participant's train and test folds by design; no leave-one-participant-out evaluation.

entries.text: The 5-fold partition unit is unspecified: the paper does not say whether folds hold out complete words/trials/utterances or frames, nor whether adjacent windows and ±200-ms contexts are grouped or guarded across fold boundaries.
entries.condition: Test-fold construction for the participant recordings; this affects temporal and lexical independence.
entries.quote: For each participant, we partitioned the recorded data into disjoint sets for training and testing in a 5-fold cross validation.

entries.text: DenseNet initialization seeds, data-loader seeds, and independent repeated model-training runs are not reported; the 60 repetitions described are chance-baseline randomizations, not stated model repetitions.
entries.condition: Per-participant 5-fold DenseNet evaluation and chance estimation.

entries.text: The 20% validation subset is said to analyze optimization, but its use for checkpoint selection, hyperparameter selection, or early stopping is not specified.
entries.condition: Participant-specific DenseNet; fixed 80-epoch training is reported, but no validation-based selection rule is stated.
entries.quote: Twenty percent of the training data are reserved as a separate validation set to analyze the optimization process of the network training.

entries.text: Although electrode-wise zero-mean/unit-variance normalization is stated, the source of those statistics (training fold only versus all recording data) is not specified; no separate target-logMel normalization procedure is described.
entries.condition: Potential train/test preprocessing scope for ECoG inputs and regression targets.
entries.quote: We normalized broadband-gamma activity of each electrode individually to zero mean and unit variance.

entries.text: The significance test or procedure yielding p < 0.001 is not identified, and no exact STOI values are printed in the text or table.
entries.condition: Correlation significance and waveform intelligibility assessment; Figure 5c displays STOI bars without numerical labels.
entries.quote: We achieve correlations significantly better than chance level (p<0.001) for all six participants

entries.text: The exact number of unique words, lexical overlap across train/test folds, and per-fold test word composition are not reported; the stimulus set is only described as mostly Modified Rhyme Test words.
entries.condition: Single-word reading benchmark and held-out test folds.

entries.text: The number of recording sessions per participant and whether folds cross session boundaries are not reported; the paper gives only total recording duration per participant.
entries.condition: ECoG and acoustic recordings made during awake craniotomy; 8.5–12.7 minutes recorded per participant.

entries.text: No use-time language model, lexicon, textual decoder, user confirmation, or correction mechanism is described; the reported output path is spectrogram-conditioned waveform synthesis.
entries.condition: Overt speech reconstruction pipeline described in Secs. 2.3–2.5; no interactive closed-loop use was evaluated.

entries.text: The linked repository's LJSpeech configuration uses a 4.41% utterance-level test holdout and fixed split random_state 1234; its training and evaluation scripts apply/use that test partition. The paper does not pin this preset or report its vocoder split/seed, so this is a repository condition, not a confirmed study-run setting.
entries.condition: LJSpeech vocoder recipe in inspected repository snapshot 2092a647e60ce002389818de1fa66d0a2c5763d8; random_state controls data partitioning, not model initialization.

entries.text: The repository's LJSpeech preset resamples audio to 22,050 Hz, uses 80 mel bins over 125–7,600 Hz, peak-rescales each utterance to 0.999, and maps log-mel values to [0,1]. The paper does not identify this preset or its overrides; these are code defaults rather than verified settings of the reported run.
entries.unit: Hz; bins; mel limits in Hz; waveform peak; normalized range
entries.condition: LJSpeech WaveNet preprocessing/configuration in inspected repository snapshot 2092a647e60ce002389818de1fa66d0a2c5763d8; the paper separately specifies 16 kHz/40 bins for the ECoG regression target.

entries.text: Concurrent ECoG sentence synthesis (Anumanchipalli 2019) evaluated by listener transcription: median 31% WER with a 25-word pool.
entries.condition: listener transcription of synthesized sentences, 25-word pool
entries.quote: Transcribed sentences had a median 31% WER with a 25-word pool size

entries.text: Compared MLP, DenseNet (DN), and sequence-to-sequence (S2S) speech-reconstruction models.
entries.condition: Models reconstruct speech spectrograms from HD ECoG neural activity.

entries.text: Five human subjects produced 12 unique Dutch words, each repeated 10 times, in a word-production task using sensorimotor HD ECoG.
entries.condition: HD ECoG over sensorimotor cortex; overt word production.

entries.text: DN had significantly higher Pearson correlations than MLP and S2S (H=14.26); the provided text omits the pairwise PCC values, so an absolute margin cannot be recovered. DN was not a universal winner: S2S was associated with perceptual word-identifiability judgments, but the text does not establish that S2S significantly beat DN on that test.
entries.value: DN > MLP and S2S for Pearson correlation; H=14.26; absolute PCC difference not given
entries.condition: Optimized models; comparisons across subjects. Pairwise statistics are partly missing in the supplied text extraction.
entries.loc: Discussion, optimized complex model architectures; Results, low-level measures

entries.text: The paper says DN occasionally outperformed S2S, with marginal gains; it does not report a single architecture as best on every metric.
entries.condition: Discussion of Pearson correlation and other performance measures.

entries.text: Word identification by classifiers trained on target speech and tested on reconstructed speech reached 92–100% accuracy; chance was 8%.
entries.condition: Classification among 12 words; audio reconstructions from all subjects and models.

entries.text: Human listener word-identification judgments averaged 58–66% accuracy, against 50% chance.
entries.condition: Behavioral binary word-choice judgments on synthesized reconstructed speech; some S3 models and all S4 models were exceptions to above-chance identification.

entries.text: Testing used leave-one-word-out cross-validation: one of the 12 test words was left out of training per fold, using the optimized parameters; validation data was added to the training data.
entries.condition: One repetition per word was initially selected for the test set; each held-out test word was reconstructed in its own retraining fold.

entries.text: Compared 3D ResNet, 3D Swin Transformer, and LSTM ECoG decoders; the ResNet and Swin architectures use 3D operations/convolution.
